title: Empatica Embrace seizure alert reaches Morgan McGrath's mother, who calls paramedics after a seizure left the 26-year-old teacher not breathing (Fulton, Missouri)
summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that left Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Missouri, not breathing and alerted her mother, who called paramedics; IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
account: Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”, Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics, and “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. Dolgin writes that the device records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text or call to pre-specified caregivers. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The same article reports a case described by Empatica co-founder Rosalind Picard and colleagues, in which the alert reached a 20-year-old's family but nobody arrived for 15 minutes and he died. In a later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021), Empatica staff with hospital co-authors report the sensitivity of a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. In an independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026), the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on the IEEE Spectrum article alone. No second account of the McGrath event is among the sources. The Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) is not among them either.
purpose: Built to detect convulsive seizures from electrodermal activity and motion and to summon designated caregivers. The alert to McGrath's mother was that purpose.
system: Empatica Embrace wrist-worn seizure detection (electrodermal activity and accelerometer, on-board algorithm) with the Alert smartphone app
model_version: Embrace (the article does not state the generation); echoes concern Embrace2
segment: Prescription wearable seizure monitor used at home

brief: In November 2016 Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, had an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive and not breathing.[1] Her Embrace wristband detected the seizure and alerted her mother, who called paramedics. McGrath survived, and her rescue rests on a single IEEE Spectrum report. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared the device on 26 January 2018, after the event.[2] Later evidence comes from hospital epilepsy monitoring units. In an independent study published on 7 January 2026, researchers in Montreal found that the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working, with 29 false alarms in 373 days of monitoring. It detected none of 510 focal seizures without convulsions, a type that the device is not cleared to detect.[3]

data.retained_case_account: Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018 on Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri. She “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics, and “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The article says it records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text or call to pre-specified caregivers. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. A later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021) by Empatica staff with hospital co-authors reports sensitivity for a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. An independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026) found the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures while worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on this single news item. The Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) is not among the sources. No second account of the McGrath event was found.

Empatica is the author of the 510(k) summary filed with the Food and Drug Administration, and Empatica staff are the lead authors of the 2021 study by Onorati et al. The 2026 Montreal study by Jahani et al. Is independent of the maker.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: An Embrace wristband detected a seizure that left Morgan McGrath, 26, of Fulton, Missouri, not breathing and alerted her mother, who called paramedics; IEEE Spectrum reports that she survived.
fields.account: Morgan McGrath, a 26-year-old teacher from Fulton, Missouri, “suffered an epileptic seizure that left her unresponsive, frothing at the mouth, with blue lips, and not breathing”, Elie Dolgin reported in IEEE Spectrum on 6 February 2018. The article dates the seizure to “fifteen months ago”, about November 2016. Her wrist-worn Embrace device alerted her mother, who called the paramedics, and “thanks to a timely response, McGrath is alive and well today”. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared Embrace (Empatica S.r.l.) under 510(k) K172935 on 26 January 2018, after the McGrath event. The 510(k) summary describes an on-board algorithm validated against video electroencephalography (EEG). On detecting a likely generalized tonic-clonic seizure, it messages the Alert app to call and text designated caregivers. Dolgin writes that the device records skin conductance and three-axis accelerometer data and “uses a proprietary algorithm to signal when someone is having a convulsive seizure”. The app sends a text or call to pre-specified caregivers. In testing on 135 patients over more than 6,500 hours it “correctly identified nearly every single seizure”. The same article reports a case described by Empatica co-founder Rosalind Picard and colleagues, in which the alert reached a 20-year-old's family but nobody arrived for 15 minutes and he died. In a later prospective multicenter study (Onorati et al. 2021), Empatica staff with hospital co-authors report the sensitivity of a predefined machine-learning algorithm. It was 0.92 in children and 0.94 in adults. In an independent Montreal epilepsy-monitoring-unit study (Jahani et al. 2026), the Embrace2 detected all 16 convulsive seizures that occurred while it was worn and working. Alerts reached caregivers in 15 of 16 cases, with 29 false alarms. The McGrath rescue rests on the IEEE Spectrum article alone. No second account of the McGrath event is among the sources. The Empatica case-study abstract (Regalia, Onorati, Picard, American Epilepsy Society) is not among them either.
